Chart

title: Week 8 — Introduction to Machine Learning for Economics
text:
Week 7 introduced:

regression
predictive modeling
explanatory relationships
econometric thinking

Now students transition into:
machine learning
This is one of the most dangerous weeks pedagogically.
Why?
Because students are heavily exposed online to:

AI hype
buzzwords
unrealistic claims
“black-box magic”

This week is NOT about fake AI excitement.
This week is about:

conceptual clarity
analytical skepticism
computational understanding

Students must understand:

what machine learning actually is
how it differs from econometrics
why prediction matters
what overfitting means
why models fail
how ML supports economics

title: Week 2 — Working with Data in Python
text:
In Week 1, we learned how to use Python as a calculator and how to execute simple commands.
This week, we begin working with the most important asset in modern economics:
DATA
Every day economists use data to answer questions such as:

Why are some people unemployed?
What determines wages?
Why does inflation increase?
Which districts experience higher poverty?
How does education affect earnings?
How does technology influence productivity?

Regardless of whether you become:

an economist
policy analyst
researcher
consultant
banker
data analyst

your ability to work with data will become increasingly important.
For this reason, Week 2 focuses on understanding how Python stores and organizes data.
Everything we do later in the course:

data visualization
dashboards
forecasting
machine learning
artificial intelligence

depends on concepts introduced this week.

title: ECN 4199 — Industrial Data Analytics
text:
Welcome to the course website for ECN 4199: Industrial Data Analytics.
This course introduces students to modern computational and analytical tools increasingly used in:

economics
business analytics
policy analysis
finance
industry research
AI-assisted decision systems

work confidently with data

interpret analytical outputs critically
communicate evidence effectively
use AI systems responsibly

In Week 1, we learned how to run Python code and perform economic calculations.
In Week 2, we learned how data are organized and how to import and inspect a real dataset.
Week 3 moves from:

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Check Your Understanding

What type of object is growth_rates?
Which value indicates a recession?
Why is the average not enough to describe the full period?

The purpose of this recap is to confirm the foundation, not reteach it.

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Economic Example: Inflation Classification



Component
Example




Input
Inflation rate


Rule
Below 5 is low; 5–15 is moderate; above 15 is high


Process
Compare the observed rate with each threshold


Output
Inflation classification



Before writing code, an analyst should be able to explain the rule clearly in words.

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Try It
inflation = 12

print(inflation > 10)
print(inflation < 5)
print(inflation == 12)

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Example: Labour Force Classification
has_job = False
seeking_work = True

if not has_job and seeking_work:
    print("Unemployed")

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Example: Policy Alert
inflation = 18
growth = -2

if inflation > 15 or growth < 0:
    print("Macroeconomic policy attention required")

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Interpretation
The value 12 is:

not below 5
less than or equal to 15

Therefore, Python returns:
Moderate inflation

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Critical Note
This is a simplified monetary classification.
Real poverty analysis may also consider:

household size
cost-of-living differences
access to education and health
housing conditions
multidimensional deprivation

Code can automate a rule, but the analyst must evaluate whether the rule is appropriate.

title: Week 3 — Programming Logic and Automation for Economic Analysis
text:
Important Distinction
Loops are valuable for learning programming logic.
For large DataFrames, later lessons will introduce more efficient pandas methods.

Question 1
Why is the average not enough to describe inflation during a crisis period?
Correct answer:
Because the average can hide extreme values, turning points, and year-to-year instability.

title: Week 5 — Exploratory Economic Analysis
